# Preface {.unnumbered}

Carbon projects are audited on numbers that come out of a geographic information system, and very few of the people who produce or check those numbers were trained to build one. The methods literature stops at the discipline boundary: it will teach you to project a raster and never mention what a verifier does with the result. The standards documents start on the far side of it: they will tell you an uncertainty deduction is required and never show you how to compute one. Practitioners reconcile the two in undocumented spreadsheets.

This book is written to close that gap. It teaches the spatial and statistical methods that forest carbon measurement and verification actually rests on, from reading a shapefile to reporting an area-adjusted emission with a defensible interval, entirely in R and entirely reproducibly. It assumes an introductory course in statistics and no prior GIS.

## Target audience {.unnumbered}

The book is written for two audiences at once, and it is honest about which parts belong to whom.

The main text is for anyone who needs the method: graduate students in forestry, environmental science and remote sensing, and analysts moving into carbon work from an adjacent field. It teaches spatial analysis and applied statistics, and it can be read straight through without reference to any crediting standard.

Interleaved with it are verification tracks, set off in tinted boxes. These carry the registry-specific material that only practitioners need: what ART-TREES, Verra and the American Carbon Registry require, where their equations are written down, and how each converts a statistic into forgone credits. They are written for analysts and technical staff at project developers and verification bodies, and for national forest monitoring teams.

A reader who skips every verification track still gets a complete book. Nothing in the main narrative depends on what is inside them. A reader who wants only the compliance material can read the tracks alone, though the methods will be less use without the chapters around them.

## Chapter outline {.unnumbered}

The first six chapters build the spatial toolkit, each teaching a foundational concept and closing on a worked problem from a real verification project.

1. Getting Started: reproducible projects, the spatial stack, vector versus raster, a first map and coordinate check.
2. Vector Data: geometries, attributes and support, spatial joins; closing on an area check.
3. Raster Data: grids, map algebra, reclassification, extraction; closing on land-cover reclassification.
4. Terrain and Hydrology: elevation, slope and aspect, flow; closing on inundation mapping.
5. LiDAR and Point Clouds: returns, ground and canopy, tree detection; closing on a LiDAR forest inventory.
6. Disturbance and Risk: change detection, accuracy assessment, risk modelling; closing on VM0048 risk and ACR accuracy.

The next four turn that toolkit on the accounting problem, and are where the book departs from every other R-spatial text.

7. Allometry and Biomass: equation form and selection, extrapolation, wood density, scaling to the stand.
8. Emission Factors: tiers, the stock-difference method, factor selection, propagation in quadrature.
9. Activity Data and Classification: IPCC approaches, training design, probability surfaces, active learning.
10. Baseline Modelling: counterfactuals, reference periods, the ratchet, risk-weighted allocation.

The last three quantify and close.

11. Uncertainty: sampling error, accuracy metrics, cross-validation, Monte Carlo propagation, area-adjusted accuracy, and how three registries turn one statistic into three different deductions.
12. Time Series: space-time cubes, seasonality and randomness, sampling and aliasing; closing on IPCC Tier 1 fire emissions.
13. Spatial Patterns: point patterns, intensity, nearest-neighbour, Ripley's K; closing on post-fire conifer regeneration.

An appendix covers the surrounding discipline: reproducible runtimes, spatial-data protocols, and registry practice.

## Input datasets {.unnumbered}

One plot anchors the book: the Smithsonian ForestGEO census at the Conservation Biology Institute in Front Royal, Virginia, recording 38,517 living stems across 39 genera in a 400 by 640 metre footprint, each identified to species and measured for diameter. It carries the vector, allometry, biomass and error chapters.

Four further datasets, each real and each committed so the book builds offline, carry the chapters the plot cannot answer.

The raster, activity data and disturbance chapters run on a 2022 Sentinel-2 land-cover map of Rondonia, Brazil, with a matching vegetation index composite and a validation sample of 2,032 points. Labelled disturbance classes make it possible to measure what an index threshold actually catches rather than assume it.

The terrain and hydrology chapter runs on Lake Chilwa in southern Malawi: an elevation model on a 100 metre grid, with the lake, its catchment and its river network from HydroSHEDS. Chilwa is endorheic, so it is a genuine test of watershed delineation rather than a demonstration, and it is the reference case for wetland inundation mapping.

The LiDAR chapter runs on airborne laser tiles distributed with the `lidR` package, real surveys over real terrain, so ground classification, terrain interpolation and tree detection are performed rather than described.

The spatial patterns chapter runs on the published coordinates of a post-fire conifer regeneration survey in the Selkirk Mountains of British Columbia [@murphy2026selkirk].

Published allometric equations and a set of oaks with biomass computed five ways support the allometry chapter, because the cost of choosing an equation cannot be shown without several equations.

::: callout-note
## Secondary sources

Every dataset above is real and is committed to the repository, and two scripts under `data-raw/` rebuild the derived ones from their sources. Within-plot coordinates for the ForestGEO stems were generated across the real footprint because the source census table omitted them, so those maps are representative rather than a survey of record; this is stated again where they are used.

A small number of illustrative surfaces are constructed rather than observed, in order to isolate one effect at a time. Each says so where it is built, and none carries a reported number.

The keystone closings and verification tracks describe workflows from real verification projects, and reproduce their analytical core on this shared data.
:::

## User guides {.unnumbered}

Each chapter is a self-contained lesson that builds on the last. Code is shown in full and is meant to be run; the fastest way to learn is to work through it line by line and then attempt the exercises.

Every figure and every number in the text is generated by code that ships with the book and runs offline. Nothing is quoted from a source that cannot be re-executed, and where a registry document is cited the citation is to the equation and section, so a reader can check it against the original. Any package the book uses can be installed from CRAN in one command.

Readers who want a deeper or more general treatment of the spatial methods are well served by the canonical texts in the field [@pebesma2023sds; @lovelace2019geocomputation; @bivand2013asdar], and the `sf` and `terra` packages that underpin the modern R-spatial stack are described by @pebesma2018sf and @hijmans2024terra. Where the applied material touches forest-carbon conventions it follows @ipcc2006gl and the 2019 Refinement [@ipcc2019refinement].
